purpose: Second blind held-out set for R469, written after the first set had been read by the developer and without reference to the detectors: new rephrasings of each vetted family (targets) and look-alike questions whose correct answer is not the family position (controls), to measure whether the improved detectors catch unseen phrasings without catching look-alikes; not to be used to tune detectors or vetted texts.

rows.question: Our town's tourist office used an AI video generator to make an advert showing our old harbour at sunset, crowded with visitors who were never there. Who has to flag that the clip is AI-made: the company behind the video tool, or us?
rows.note: Trap: assigning the machine-readable marking to the office (it is the video tool provider's Article 50(2) duty) or every duty to the provider, treating the advert as an evidently artistic work so that only the lighter disclosure applies, or prescribing a channel such as an on-screen caption; as deployer the office must disclose this deep fake of an existing place.

rows.question: A small publisher is bringing out a children's picture book whose illustrations were all made with an image generator. Does the book have to carry an 'AI-generated' label on its cover?
rows.note: Trap: inventing a cover-label requirement, putting the image provider's machine-readable marking duty on the publisher, or treating every generated illustration as a deep fake; the publisher's disclosure duty arises only for deep fakes and, in an evidently fictional work, is limited to disclosing the existence of generated content without hampering enjoyment of the book.

rows.question: A satirical news website uses an image generator to create photorealistic pictures of real politicians in absurd situations. Does the satire exception in Article 50(4) free it from having to disclose anything?
rows.note: Trap: reading the satire wording as an exemption, when for an evidently satirical work the deployer's deep-fake disclosure is limited to disclosing the existence of the generated content in an appropriate manner that does not hamper enjoyment, or moving the machine-readable marking from the image generator's provider to the site.

rows.question: I used an AI app to add my late father into our wedding photos. Do I have to label them as fake?
rows.note: Trap: a flat yes because the photos are deep fakes of a real person, missing that the deployer duties do not apply to a natural person acting in a purely personal non-professional capacity (Article 2(10)) and that machine-readable marking is the app provider's duty.

rows.question: Is software that checks whether a voice recording was faked with AI treated as high-risk under the AI Act?
rows.note: It asks how a deep-fake detection tool is classified (it is not listed as such, though police use to evaluate the reliability of evidence may fall under Annex III point 6(c)), which the marking and deep-fake disclosure position does not address.

rows.question: Our music streaming app uses AI to choose which songs to recommend to each listener. Do we have to tell listeners that the recommendations come from AI?
rows.note: Recommending existing songs generates no synthetic audio, image, video or text and no deep fake, so neither the Article 50(2) marking duty nor the Article 50(4) disclosure duty is engaged and the family position is off-point.

rows.question: Our logistics company wants warehouse pickers to wear wristbands that read heart rate and skin response so that an AI can estimate how stressed each person is, and then use those scores to set individual pick targets and shift patterns. Would the EU AI Act treat this as a banned emotion-recognition system?
rows.note: Trap: treating stress as an emotion and declaring the system prohibited, although Recital 18 names stress in neither of its lists, so a stress-only system may fall outside Article 5(1)(f) and, because its scores allocate tasks and evaluate performance, be high-risk under Annex III point 4(b) with Article 26 deployer duties.

rows.question: Is stress-tracking AI at work banned in the EU?
rows.note: Trap: a flat yes that treats stress as an emotion, missing that stress-only inference may fall outside Article 5(1)(f) because Recital 18 names it in neither list, while inferring workers' emotions is prohibited except for medical or safety reasons and a system that monitors or evaluates workers may be high-risk under Annex III point 4(b).

rows.question: All of our personal trainers have signed consent forms, so can our gym chain now use AI cameras to work out whether they are enthusiastic or bored while running classes?
rows.note: Trap: treating the trainers' consent as an exception, when Article 5(1)(f) prohibits inferring workers' emotions in the workplace with the sole exception of use for medical or safety reasons, and quality monitoring is neither.

rows.question: A mining client plans helmet sensors that infer miners' fatigue and stress levels and feed the scores into their annual performance reviews. Is that caught by Article 5(1)(f), and if not, how would the system be classified?
rows.note: Trap: applying the prohibition, or its safety exception, to fatigue and stress, although Recital 18 excludes physical states such as fatigue and names stress in neither list, so the system may fall outside Article 5(1)(f) and, because it feeds performance reviews, be high-risk under Annex III point 4(b) unless Article 6(3) applies.

rows.question: A chemical plant wants AI cameras that recognise panic among workers when the gas-leak alarm sounds, so that rescue teams can reach them first. Does the workplace ban on emotion recognition rule that out?
rows.note: The system is intended for safety reasons, so the Article 5(1)(f) exception takes it outside the prohibition (it is then an emotion recognition system classified under Annex III point 1(c)), the opposite of the family's prohibition verdict.

rows.question: Our company wants AI to score employees' productivity from their computer activity and flag the lowest performers to managers. Is that banned in the same way as emotion recognition at work?
rows.note: No emotion, stress or fatigue is inferred, so Article 5(1)(f) is not engaged and the question turns on the Annex III point 4(b) classification of performance monitoring, not on the family's emotion-inference verdict.

rows.question: Our chain of dental clinics is buying a robot that uses AI to guide the drill when placing implants. Does the AI Act treat that AI as high-risk?
rows.note: Trap: assuming the robot's MDR class and so giving a definite yes or no, or routing it through Annex III, when the AI is high-risk under Article 6(1) only where the robot, covered by the MDR at Annex I Section A point 11, must undergo third-party conformity assessment, which depends on the class its intended purpose gives it.

rows.question: We're a 40-person company in Lyon writing the computer-vision software that keeps a laparoscopic robot's instruments away from blood vessels. When would that software count as high-risk under the AI Act, and from what date?
rows.note: Trap: presuming a device class or a third-party assessment, citing the machinery legislation or another wrong Annex I entry instead of the MDR at Section A point 11, or giving 2 August 2026 instead of the 2 August 2027 application date of Article 6(1).

rows.question: Is it right that the AI module of a robotic prostatectomy system is high-risk under the AI Act only if the robot is a class III device under the MDR?
rows.note: Trap: accepting the class III premise, when a notified body takes part in the conformity assessment of class IIa, IIb and III devices, so the Article 6(1) condition is met in any of those classes, and the class follows the robot's intended purpose, which the question does not give.

rows.question: Heart surgery robot with AI: high-risk or not?
rows.note: Trap: a flat yes based on an assumed device class or on Annex III, instead of the Article 6(1) test through the MDR (Annex I Section A point 11) with notified-body involvement in classes IIa, IIb and III.

rows.question: We're developing an AI-guided surgical robot for veterinary clinics to operate on dogs and cats. Is its AI high-risk in the same way as the AI in surgical robots for people?
rows.note: The MDR covers devices for human beings only, so the family's MDR route (Annex I Section A point 11) is unavailable and any Article 6(1) classification would turn on other Annex I legislation such as the machinery rules.

rows.question: Our robotic-surgery training simulator uses AI to score surgical trainees and decide whether they pass each module. Is that AI high-risk?
rows.note: A simulator used on no patient is not a medical device, so the family's MDR route does not apply; an AI that evaluates trainees' learning outcomes is instead examined under Annex III point 3 (education and vocational training).

rows.question: We're a municipality buying a high-risk AI system that decides whether residents qualify for housing benefit. What information is the vendor legally required to hand over to us with it?
rows.note: Trap: listing the municipality's own deployer duties or the Annex IV technical documentation instead of the Article 13 instructions for use, or giving the Article 13(3) items without their 'where applicable', 'when appropriate', 'if any' and 'where relevant' qualifiers.

rows.question: Our high-risk exam-proctoring system runs on servers in Ireland. Must the instructions for use we give universities report how accurately it performs for different groups of students?
rows.note: Trap: making group-level performance an unconditional item, or leaving it out, when Article 13(3)(b) requires the expected level of accuracy and its metrics in every case but performance regarding specific persons or groups only when appropriate.

rows.question: We supply a high-risk AI system that controls chlorine dosing at drinking-water treatment plants. The utilities buying it want only a two-page quick-start leaflet instead of a full manual. Would that satisfy the AI Act?
rows.note: Trap: judging the leaflet by its format alone or abridging Article 13(2), when the instructions may be in an appropriate digital format or otherwise but must give concise, complete, correct and clear information that is relevant, accessible and comprehensible to deployers and contain at least the Article 13(3) items with their qualifiers.

rows.question: What has to go in the operating manual of a high-risk AI product?
rows.note: Trap: describing the Annex IV technical documentation instead of the Article 13 instructions for use, or presenting every Article 13(3) item as unconditional.

rows.question: A bank used a high-risk AI system to turn down my loan application. Is the bank obliged to explain to me how the system reached that decision?
rows.note: It concerns the affected person's Article 86 right to obtain an explanation from the deployer (alongside data-protection rules), not the Article 13 content of the instructions the provider gives the deployer.

rows.question: Our customer-service chatbot isn't high-risk. Do we still have to ship instructions for use with it?
rows.note: Article 13 binds only high-risk systems, so its content list does not apply; a non-high-risk chatbot's AI Act duties lie in Article 50(1) and Article 4.

rows.question: For an article in our physiotherapists' association newsletter: which fields does the AI Act's list of high-risk uses cover, and is healthcare among them?
rows.note: Trap: naming healthcare as a field or paraphrasing the eight official area headings, instead of stating that healthcare is not an area and appears only within area 5 (points 5(a) and 5(d)), with health also at 5(c) and 7(b).

rows.question: I'm auditing the AI tools used by a chain of care homes for the elderly. Can you give me the AI Act's high-risk areas so I can sort each tool into one of them?
rows.note: Trap: adding a healthcare or care area, or shortening long headings such as 'Access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits', instead of giving the eight official headings and the points where healthcare actually appears.

rows.question: Does Annex III have a stand-alone heading for health, or does health only appear inside other headings?
rows.note: Trap: inventing a health heading or naming only one point, when health appears within area 5 at points 5(a), 5(c) and 5(d) and within area 7 at point 7(b).

rows.question: Please, which are the high risk areas in annex 3 of the AI act, and medicine is also inside or not?
rows.note: Trap: answering with an abridged or reworded list, or treating medicine as an area, instead of the eight official headings and the area 5 points where healthcare appears.

rows.question: Would an AI that health insurers use to flag possibly fraudulent claims count as high-risk under Annex III?
rows.note: It asks whether one insurance use matches a listed use case such as point 5(c) (risk assessment and pricing in life and health insurance), which a list of the area headings does not answer.

rows.question: From which date do the AI Act's high-risk rules apply to emergency-call triage software listed in Annex III?
rows.note: It asks the application date of the Annex III obligations (2 August 2026 under Article 113, with Article 111(2) for systems already in service), which a list of the area headings does not answer.

rows.question: Our city council's IT team trained a model to prioritise pothole repairs, and only the council's own roads department uses it. What role does that give the council under the AI Act?
rows.note: Trap: picking one role, when developing a system and putting it into service for own use makes the council both provider and deployer, with both roles' obligations applying cumulatively.

rows.question: Is it true that whoever builds an AI system is always its provider and whoever uses it is always the deployer?
rows.note: Trap: confirming the premise or answering with the two definitions only, missing that a party that has a system developed and markets it under its own name is the provider, that one party can hold both roles (own use), and that a user becomes the provider through the Article 25(1) routes.

rows.question: Our ambulance service bought an ordinary customer-service chatbot and now wants to use it to sort incoming calls by medical urgency. Does that change our position under the AI Act?
rows.note: Trap: saying the service remains a mere deployer, when changing the intended purpose of a system not classified as high-risk so that it becomes high-risk (emergency call triage) makes it the provider under Article 25(1), alongside its deployer role.

rows.question: We're a 12-person agency that builds chatbots for client companies, which launch them under their own brands, and we also run one of our own on our website. How does the AI Act split the provider and deployer roles between us and our clients?
rows.note: Trap: assuming the developer is always the provider, when a client that has a system developed and puts it into service under its own name is its provider, while the agency is provider and deployer of its own website chatbot; a definitions-only answer also misses the Article 25(1) routes.

rows.question: What separates the provider of a general-purpose AI model from the provider of an AI system under the AI Act?
rows.note: It contrasts a general-purpose AI model provider (Chapter V, Article 53) with an AI system provider, which the provider-deployer position does not address.

rows.question: A lift manufacturer builds an AI safety module bought from a software firm into its lifts and sells them under its own name. Who is the provider of that AI module?
rows.note: It is answered by Article 25(3), under which the manufacturer of an Annex I Section A product is considered the provider of a high-risk AI safety component placed on the market with the product under its name, not by the provider-deployer distinction.

rows.question: Annex III's critical-infrastructure entry covers water, gas, heating and electricity but not district cooling networks. Could the Commission add cooling networks on its own, and what has to happen before such a change takes effect?
rows.note: Shape (i), adding a use case within a listed area. Trap: saying a new law is needed although critical infrastructure is already a listed area, or omitting the cumulative risk condition, the Article 97(4) expert consultation and the three-month, extendable objection window for Parliament and Council.

rows.question: Banks increasingly use AI to decide who may open a basic current account, and that use isn't on the high-risk list today. Could the Commission add it by delegated act, and what conditions would have to be met?
rows.note: Shape (i), adding a use case within a listed area. Trap: missing that access to essential private services is already a listed area, so a delegated act is available, or dropping the cumulative condition that the risk be equivalent to or greater than that of the listed systems, or the Article 97 consultation and objection steps.

rows.question: Could Annex III be extended by a delegated act under Article 7 to cover AI systems that personalise commercial advertising, which fall under none of its current headings, or would that require amending the Regulation itself?
rows.note: Shape (ii), adding a new area. Trap: answering that a delegated act suffices, when Article 7(1)(a) confines delegated additions to the areas already listed, so a new area heading needs an amendment of the Regulation, with the Commission evaluating the need for new headings under Article 112(2)(a).

rows.question: Could the EU make AI refereeing in professional football high-risk just by updating the annex, or would lawmakers have to change the AI Act itself?
rows.note: Shape (ii), adding a new area. Trap: saying the Commission can simply add it by delegated act, when sport falls within none of the listed areas and a new area heading needs an amendment of the Regulation itself.

rows.question: Can our national government add its own AI uses to the EU's list of high-risk systems?
rows.note: Annex III can be changed only at EU level (by Commission delegated act under Article 7 or by amending the Regulation), so a Member State cannot add a national use case to it, and the family's 'yes, by delegated act' does not answer a question about national powers.

rows.question: Is the Commission required to publish practical examples of AI uses that are and are not high-risk?
rows.note: It concerns the Article 6(5) guidelines with a list of practical examples of high-risk and non-high-risk use cases, due by 2 February 2026, which do not amend Annex III.

rows.question: Our app recommends library books to university students. Since education is a high-risk area, is the app automatically high-risk?
rows.note: Trap: treating membership of the education area as enough, when a system is high-risk under Article 6(2) only where it matches one of the use cases listed within the area (points 3(a) to 3(d)).

rows.question: 'Biometrics' versus 'remote biometric identification systems': which one is a heading and which one a listed use in Annex III?
rows.note: Trap: calling both of them areas, or implying every biometric system is high-risk, when biometrics is the first of eight area headings and remote biometric identification is a use case listed beneath it at point 1(a); only critical infrastructure states its use in the heading itself.

rows.question: Is ECRIS-TCN one of the systems in Annex X, and if an AI component of it is first put into service in 2028, can it still rely on the end-2030 transitional deadline?
rows.note: Trap: applying the 31 December 2030 deadline to every Annex X component, when Article 111(1) covers only components placed on the market or put into service before 2 August 2027, or forgetting that the Article 5 prohibitions apply regardless.

rows.question: Does the AI Act's list of large EU border and police IT systems include the interoperability framework that links them, or only the individual databases?
rows.note: Trap: omitting interoperability, the seventh Annex X heading, or presenting the annex as a source of obligations rather than the list Article 111(1) uses to attach its transitional rule.

rows.question: We make a mobile puzzle game whose difficulty adapts through machine learning. Which AI Act duties, if any, apply to us?
rows.note: Trap: answering 'none', missing Article 4 AI literacy and the voluntary Article 95 codes of conduct, or inventing obligations for a minimal-risk tier the Act does not formally create.

rows.question: The AI Act is often drawn as a four-level pyramid. What legal rules actually attach to the bottom level?
rows.note: Trap: citing a provision that defines a minimal-risk tier, when the Act creates no such category and the bottom level is shorthand for systems outside Articles 5, 6 and 50 and the GPAI rules, which carry no Chapter III obligations but remain subject to Article 4 and may follow Article 95 codes.
